new.title: Eat lunch at the volunteer-run Wasven farm
new.desc: Hidden in the Tongelre district, the Wasven farm was built by Philips in 1941 on an estate first cleared in the thirteenth century. Locals saved it from sale in the 2000s, and it now holds an organic restaurant, a traditional bakery and a market garden set in six hectares of green.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays. Buy a loaf from the bakery before you leave and walk the old beech avenue towards the village heart of Tongelre.

new.title: Eat a pancake in the Philips orchard
new.desc: The Philips Fruittuin was planted in the 1930s as a job creation scheme that kept Philips workers employed through the crisis years and gave the workforce fresh fruit. After years of neglect it was restored, and since 2008 it has had a pancake house, a farm shop and a small playground among the apple and pear trees.
new.tip: The orchard opens for apple and pear picking on a few days in late summer; check the dates before you cycle out. It is about four kilometres from the centre along the Oirschotsedijk.

new.title: Dine among the machines at Radio Royaal
new.desc: Radio Royaal fills the Machinekamer, the old engine room that once kept the Philips works at Strijp-S running. The kitchen cooks German and French comfort food in a big industrial hall.
new.tip: It opens Tuesday to Saturday from five in the afternoon, so plan it as dinner. It sits right across from Strijp-S station, next to the Ketelhuis and the Klokgebouw.

new.title: Share the long table at 't Rozenknopje
new.desc: Café 't Rozenknopje on the Hoogstraat is one of the oldest pubs in town and was long known as the living room of the Gestel district. It is open seven days a week, with live music on the small stage downstairs and in the nostalgic theatre hall above the bar.
new.tip: Monday is the night to come: guests eat with the locals at one long table. Ask what is on in the upstairs hall while you are there.

new.title: Taste farm cheese at the Genneper Hoeve
new.desc: The Genneper Hoeve is a biodynamic city farm in the Dommel valley, with red and white dairy cows, pigs, chickens and its own cheese dairy. The farm shop and the ProefLokaal serve coffee and lunch made largely with produce from the yard.
new.tip: Shop and ProefLokaal are open daily from 10 to 17. You may wander the farmyard freely, and with luck you will see the cows cross the path on their way to the milking parlour.

new.title: Eat between design pieces at Kazerne
new.desc: Kazerne occupies one of the first military police barracks in the Netherlands, built in 1825, together with a 1925 municipal warehouse next door. Since 2014 it has combined a restaurant and bar with changing design exhibitions, so you eat surrounded by the work of designers.
new.tip: You do not need to dine to look around; have a coffee and walk through the exhibition. Book ahead during Dutch Design Week in October.

new.title: Pick a table on the Kleine Berg
new.desc: De Bergen is one of the oldest quarters of Eindhoven, built on a few sand hills just outside the medieval town and largely spared in the Second World War. Its main street, the Kleine Berg, is lined with eetcafés, restaurants, bookshops and antique dealers in old townhouses.
new.tip: Walk the whole street and the Bergstraat side lane before choosing. Eetcafé Bommel at number 32 is a long-standing student favourite.

new.title: Lunch at the Opwetten watermill Van Gogh painted
new.desc: The watermill on the Kleine Dommel at Opwetten was first mentioned in the eleventh century and rebuilt after a fire in 1764. Vincent van Gogh painted it in 1884, and its great wheel is often called the largest in the province. The former oil and fulling mill now houses a restaurant.
new.tip: The restaurant is closed on Mondays. The grain mill across the water still works and opens to visitors on Sunday afternoons.

new.title: Drink a Vandeoirsprong beer in Oirschot's old brewery
new.desc: Beer has been brewed on the Koestraat in Oirschot for close to four centuries, most famously at brewery De Kroon, whose complex dates from 1773. Since 2015 Brouwerij Vandeoirsprong has brewed there again with water from its own well, and its tasting room and terrace fill the old buildings.
new.tip: Start with the Zwickel or the O.P.A. and look into the small brewery museum on site. The kitchen runs a changing dish of the day.

new.title: Count the seven sides of the Lichttoren
new.desc: The white, seven-sided Lichttoren rose in stages between 1909 and 1921 as part of the Philips lamp factories. Endurance tests on light bulbs were run on its top floor, and the glow could be seen far beyond the town, which is how the tower got its name.
new.tip: Come after dark, when the tower is lit with LEDs. The little statue in front is Het Lampenmaakstertje, the lamp maker girl.

new.title: Find the lone Oude Toren of Woensel
new.desc: This Gothic brick tower is all that remains of the Sint-Petruskerk of Woensel, a church from about 1440 that was pulled down in 1815. Woensel was a village of its own until Eindhoven absorbed it in 1920, and the tower marks its oldest core.
new.tip: Combine it with the Commonwealth war cemetery a few minutes north on the Baffinlaan. The tower itself is only seen from outside.

new.title: Stroll the garden village Philips built for its workers
new.desc: When the lamp factory outgrew little Eindhoven, Philips bought farmland in Strijp and from 1910 built its own village for the workers. Philipsdorp was laid out with greenery and a village feel for staff who mostly came from the countryside, and it has been a protected townscape since 2010.
new.tip: Start on the Sint Elisabethlaan, right behind the PSV stadium, and wander the side streets. People live here, so keep it to the pavements.

new.title: Look up at Eindhoven's tallest church tower
new.desc: The Sint-Joriskerk in Stratum was designed by Hendrik van Tulder and opened in 1885; the west tower by his pupil Jacobus van Gils followed in 1911. At about 88 metres it is the tallest church in the city, and you enter straight through the base of the tower.
new.tip: The best view of the tower is from the far end of the Sint Jorislaan. It is a working parish church, so the door is mostly open around services.

new.title: Cross the moat into Kasteel Helmond
new.desc: Begun around 1325, Kasteel Helmond is a square moated castle with a round tower on each corner. It served as Helmond's town hall from 1923 until 2001 and has housed Museum Helmond since 1982.
new.tip: The same museum runs the Kunsthal Helmond nearby, so ask about a combined visit. Walk once around the moat first for the classic view of the towers.

new.title: Join a guided tour of lived-in Kasteel Heeze
new.desc: Kasteel Heeze is one of the few Dutch castles that is still a family home. It joins the medieval castle Eymerick to a wing built in 1665 by the architect Pieter Post, and the guided tour takes in wall tapestries, a bath in Roman style and an original bedroom.
new.tip: Open tours usually run on Wednesday and Sunday afternoons at two o'clock from May to September and last about an hour and a quarter. Photography inside is not allowed.

new.title: Step into the hall church of Weert
new.desc: The Sint-Martinuskerk on Weert's Markt is a late Gothic hall church, one of only two of its kind left in the Netherlands. The choir was finished in 1456, the vaults carry some of the largest late Gothic ceiling paintings in the country, and the choir holds the tomb of Filips van Montmorency, Count of Horne.
new.tip: Look up before anything else: the vault paintings are the treasure here. The tower holds a large carillon that rings out over the Markt.

new.title: Learn why Valkenswaard is named after falcons
new.desc: From about 1650 to 1850 the falconers of Valkenswaard caught and trained birds of prey for the courts of Europe. The Valkerij en Sigarenmakerij Museum tells that story and the one that followed: an English falconer's legacy helped start a cigar factory here in 1865.
new.tip: The museum is run by volunteers, so check the opening times before you go. The Markt with its cafés is a few minutes' walk away.
new.q: Valkerij en Sigarenmakerij Museum, Oranje Nassaustraat 8b, Valkenswaard

new.title: Stand under the giant chair of Oirschot
new.desc: Oirschot calls its Grote Stoel the largest wooden chair in Europe. The first one was made in 1958 as a tribute to the craftsmanship of the village's furniture makers; an older version now stands in the Openluchtmuseum in Arnhem and the current chair took its place in 2009.
new.tip: It stands where the Gasthuisstraat meets the Rijkesluisstraat. Walk on to the centre for the blunt Gothic tower of the Sint-Petrusbasiliek.

new.title: Swim in the IJzeren Man lake
new.desc: The IJzeren Man was dug around 1910 as a sand pit for the new railway station and the line to Weert, and takes its name from the locals' nickname for the excavator. It has been a natural swimming pool since 1917, today with a sand beach, pedal boats and rowing boats.
new.tip: It only opens in the summer season and fills up fast on hot days, so come early.
new.q: Natuurbad De IJzeren Man, Javalaan 149, Eindhoven

new.title: Walk or run a lap of the Karpendonkse Plas
new.desc: This big lake in Tongelre was dug for the sand needed to raise the city's railway, a project finished in 1953. Today it lies in a park of pines, rhododendrons and junipers, with an island in the middle and plenty of waterfowl.
new.tip: A free weekly parkrun has circled the lake since 2020, a friendly way to meet local runners. Otherwise just take the path around the water at your own pace.

new.title: Ride the fair at Park Hilaria
new.desc: Park Hilaria is Eindhoven's ten-day summer funfair, stretched for about a kilometre along the Kennedylaan. Unlike most Dutch fairs it is fenced like a park with a main entrance, though entry is free, and it draws several hundred thousand visitors.
new.tip: It starts on the Friday before the first Sunday of August. Go on a weekday evening for shorter queues and the lights.

new.title: Walk the Philips de Jongh park
new.desc: Anton Philips and his wife Anna de Jongh gave this wooded park to the city in 1920, and it still carries her name. It lies in the north of Strijp, close to the PSV training ground, and the PSV squad comes here for its forest runs.
new.tip: Come on a quiet weekday morning for the woodland paths. The park also hosts a few festivals in summer, so check ahead if you want peace.

new.title: Watch an arthouse film at Natlab
new.desc: Natlab was the first building of the Philips physics laboratory, founded in 1914 to give the company its own inventions and patents. Since 2013 it has been a film theatre with theatre, exhibitions and talks, plus a café with outdoor seating.
new.tip: The café is a good place to wait for your film. It opens from mid afternoon on most days and earlier on Sundays.

new.title: Skate laps at the IJssportcentrum
new.desc: In the Genneper Parken lies a semi-covered 400 metre artificial ice track, with an indoor hall that is home to the Eindhoven Kemphanen ice hockey club. In the cold months it opens for public skating, and you can hire skates on the spot.
new.tip: The season usually starts in mid October. Check the public skating hours first, as clubs and lessons take up much of the ice.

new.title: Meet the sheep on the Strabrechtse Heide
new.desc: The Strabrechtse Heide near Heeze is about 1,500 hectares of heath, drift sand and fens, among them the Beuven, the largest fen on the heath. A flock of some 350 Kempen heath sheep is kept at the sheepfold of De Plaetse, where several walking routes begin.
new.tip: Start at De Plaetse, which also has a heath garden. The heather turns the plain purple in late summer.

new.title: Spend an afternoon at Weert's IJzeren Man
new.desc: Like its namesake in Eindhoven, this lake area is named after the steam excavator that dug it, here between 1910 and 1913. Around the lakes you find mixed forest, a children's farm and a swimming complex with indoor and outdoor pools.
new.tip: Bring walking shoes as well as swimming things: the woods run on into the Laurabossen and the Altweerterheide.
